claim: Inhibition modulates second order neurons in the cochlear nucleus, specifically spherical bushy cells (SBCs).
source: In the auditory system, inhibition already modulates second order neurons in the cochlear nucleus, e.g. spherical bushy cells (SBCs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about the auditory system.

claim: Inhibition is widely co-tuned with excitation in spherical bushy cells.
source: Using a combination of in vivo loose-patch recordings, iontophoretic drug application, and detailed signal analysis in the Mongolian Gerbil, we demonstrate that inhibition is widely co-tuned with excitation, and leads only to minor sharpening of the spectral response properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data from the study.

claim: Inhibition leads only to minor sharpening of the spectral response properties in SBCs.
source: Using a combination of in vivo loose-patch recordings, iontophoretic drug application, and detailed signal analysis in the Mongolian Gerbil, we demonstrate that inhibition is widely co-tuned with excitation, and leads only to minor sharpening of the spectral response properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Inhibition renders the neuronal output temporally sparser and more reproducible than the input.
source: Combinations of complex stimuli and neuronal input-output analysis based on spectrotemporal receptive fields revealed inhibition to render the neuronal output temporally sparser and more reproducible than the input.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data using complex stimuli and STRF analysis.

claim: Inhibition improves the temporal response fidelity of SBCs across a wide range of input intensities.
source: Overall, inhibition plays a central role in improving the temporal response fidelity of SBCs across a wide range of input intensities and thereby provides the basis for high-fidelity signal processing.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: In cortical processing, inhibitory neurons interact reciprocally with dominant excitatory neurons and serve key functions in shaping responses.
source: In cortical processing, the dominant excitatory neurons interact reciprocally with inhibitory neurons, which serve key functions in shaping the responses (reviewed in Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In the auditory cortex, inhibition dynamically balances excitation via a high degree of co-tuning.
source: In the auditory cortex, recent work has emphasized the role of inhibition in dynamically balancing excitation via a high degree of co-tuning (e.g. Wehr and Zador, 2003; Renart et al., 2010) that serves to shape and accelerate network dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In other sensory modalities, inhibition is co-tuned with excitation in the cortex, typically with wider tuning, generating inhibitory sidebands.
source: Similarly, in other modalities, inhibition was found to be co-tuned with excitation in the cortex, typically with a wider tuning, generating the well-described inhibitory sidebands (auditory: Wang et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2008, visual: Sohya et al., 2007; Niell and Stryker, 2008; Liu et al., 2009, 2011; Katzner et al., 2011, olfactory: Poo and Isaacson, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations across different sensory modalities.

claim: Temporally, inhibition often follows excitation closely in sensory systems.
source: Temporally, inhibition often follows excitation closely (auditory: Wehr and Zador, 2003, somatosensory: Wilent and Contreras, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in auditory and somatosensory systems.

claim: Various studies have shown prominent inhibitory influences on signal processing in the cochlear nucleus.
source: Various studies have shown prominent inhibitory influences on signal processing in the cochlear nucleus (Caspary et al., 1994; Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Gai and Carney, 2008), in the medial and lateral superior olive (Grothe and Sanes, 1993; Brand et al., 2002; Myoga et al., 2014), and in the dorsal and ventral nuclei of the lateral lemniscus (Yang and Pollak, 1994, 1998; Burger and Pollak, 2001; Nayagam et al., 2005; Pecka et al., 2007; Spencer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Spherical bushy cells in the anteroventral division of the cochlear nucleus provide temporally precise excitatory inputs to binaural neurons in the medial superior olive.
source: Spherical bushy cells (SBC) in the anteroventral division of the CN (AVCN) provide the temporally precise excitatory inputs to binaural neurons in the medial superior olive (MSO), where interaural time differences are computed (Yin and Chan, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SBCs receive suprathreshold excitatory input from auditory nerve fibers via large axosomatic terminals called endbulbs of Held.
source: These SBCs receive suprathreshold excitatory input from auditory nerve fibers (ANF) via large axosomatic terminals, the endbulbs of Held (Brawer and Morest, 1975; Schwartz and Gulley, 1978; Ryugo and Sento, 1991; Nicol and Walmsley, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Inhibitory inputs on SBCs provide surprisingly slow acoustically evoked inhibition mediated by glycine and GABA.
source: In addition, inhibitory inputs on SBCs have been reported, which provide surprisingly slow acoustically evoked inhibition mediated by glycine and GABA (Wu and Oertel, 1986; Kolston et al., 1992; Juiz et al., 1996; Lim et al., 2000; Mahendrasingam et al., 2004; Xie and Manis, 2013), with glycine dominating (Nerlich et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Glycine dominates the inhibitory inputs on SBCs.
source: In addition, inhibitory inputs on SBCs have been reported, which provide surprisingly slow acoustically evoked inhibition mediated by glycine and GABA (Wu and Oertel, 1986; Kolston et al., 1992; Juiz et al., 1996; Lim et al., 2000; Mahendrasingam et al., 2004; Xie and Manis, 2013), with glycine dominating (Nerlich et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Some studies comparing population data reported a general increase in temporal precision from ANF to neurons in the CN.
source: With respect to changes in temporal precision from ANF to neurons in the CN some studies – comparing population data – reported a general increase in temporal precision (Joris et al., 1994a, 1994b), while others found no change (Bourk, 1976; Blackburn and Sachs, 1989; Winter and Palmer, 1990), or reported decreased temporal precision at certain stimulation frequencies (Paolini et al., 2001; Fukui et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some studies found no change in temporal precision from ANF to neurons in the CN.
source: With respect to changes in temporal precision from ANF to neurons in the CN some studies – comparing population data – reported a general increase in temporal precision (Joris et al., 1994a, 1994b), while others found no change (Bourk, 1976; Blackburn and Sachs, 1989; Winter and Palmer, 1990), or reported decreased temporal precision at certain stimulation frequencies (Paolini et al., 2001; Fukui et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some studies reported decreased temporal precision at certain stimulation frequencies from ANF to neurons in the CN.
source: With respect to changes in temporal precision from ANF to neurons in the CN some studies – comparing population data – reported a general increase in temporal precision (Joris et al., 1994a, 1994b), while others found no change (Bourk, 1976; Blackburn and Sachs, 1989; Winter and Palmer, 1990), or reported decreased temporal precision at certain stimulation frequencies (Paolini et al., 2001; Fukui et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent studies comparing endbulb-evoked EPSPs with SBC action potentials revealed a slight increase in temporal precision of signal coding, attributed to acoustically evoked inhibition.
source: The respective experiments revealed a slight increase in temporal precision of signal coding, attributed to the influence of acoustically evoked inhibition (Dehmel et al., 2010; Kuenzel et al., 2011; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fast inhibition in T stellate cells has been attributed to a role in comodulation masking release.
source: While fast inhibition in T stellate cells has been attributed to a role in comodulation masking release (Pressnitzer et al., 2001), the inhibitory dynamics in SBCs seem to be too slow for such an effect (Xie and Manis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The inhibitory dynamics in SBCs are too slow for comodulation masking release.
source: While fast inhibition in T stellate cells has been attributed to a role in comodulation masking release (Pressnitzer et al., 2001), the inhibitory dynamics in SBCs seem to be too slow for such an effect (Xie and Manis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Inhibition functions as a gain control that renders the postsynaptic response sparser in time and more reproducible across trials.
source: While we observed some sharpening of the response in time and frequency, our results suggest that inhibition functions as a gain control that renders the postsynaptic response sparser in time and more reproducible across trials.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction based on the study's results.

claim: Temporal sparsity can increase the information per spike while reducing energy expenditure.
source: Temporal sparsity, i.e. a response restricted to fewer time-points, can increase the information per spike while reducing the energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the introduction, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Reproducibility provides reliable stimulus encoding.
source: Reproducibility, i.e. a more consistent response to identical stimuli, can provide reliable stimulus encoding.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the introduction.

claim: The subtractive component of glycinergic inhibition enhances temporal sparsity by raising the threshold for spiking.
source: These improvements are a consequence of the combined subtractive/divisive action of glycine (Kuenzel et al., 2011, 2015): The subtractive component enhances the temporal sparsity by raising the threshold for spiking.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The divisive component of glycinergic inhibition acts primarily as a gain control.
source: The divisive component acts primarily as a gain control, which - in conjunction with the co-tuning - maintains the SBC output rate in a smaller range across different stimulus levels.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A total of 85 units were recorded from the rostral pole of the anteroventral cochlear nucleus.
source: A total of 85 units were recorded from the rostral pole of the anteroventral cochlear nucleus (AVCN), the location of large, low-frequency coding SBCs (Bazwinsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: The rostral pole of the AVCN is the location of large, low-frequency coding SBCs.
source: A total of 85 units were recorded from the rostral pole of the anteroventral cochlear nucleus (AVCN), the location of large, low-frequency coding SBCs (Bazwinsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SBCs were identified based on a discernible prepotential in addition to the complex waveform.
source: The identification of SBCs was based on the following physiological properties: a discernible prepotential in addition to the complex waveform (Pfeiffer, 1966; Englitz et al., 2009; Typlt et al., 2010), short AP duration (Typlt et al., 2012), high spontaneous firing rates (Smith et al., 1993), and the primary like response pattern to pure-tone stimulation (Blackburn and Sachs, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: From the 85 cells recorded, 23 were recorded while simultaneously applying glycine receptor agonists and antagonists.
source: From these 85 cells, 23 were recorded while simultaneously applying glycine receptor agonists and antagonists.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: Units had a characteristic frequency of 2.1 ± 0.6 kHz.
source: Units had a characteristic frequency (CF) of (mean ± standard deviation) 2.1 ± 0.6 kHz and a minimal threshold of (median [first quartile, third quartile]) 7.5 [0.8, 14.9] dB SPL.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: Units had a minimal threshold of 7.5 [0.8, 14.9] dB SPL.
source: Units had a characteristic frequency (CF) of (mean ± standard deviation) 2.1 ± 0.6 kHz and a minimal threshold of (median [first quartile, third quartile]) 7.5 [0.8, 14.9] dB SPL.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: During spontaneous activity, EPSP amplitudes are close to threshold, such that not all ANF input spikes trigger an SBC output spike.
source: Previous studies showed that during spontaneous activity, EPSP amplitudes are close to threshold, such that not all ANF input spikes trigger an SBC output spike.
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous studies.

claim: Acoustically evoked inhibition interacts dynamically with the EPSPs and prevents output spikes.
source: Also, acoustically evoked inhibition interacts dynamically with the EPSPs and prevents output spikes (Kuenzel et al., 2011; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The maximum falling slope was consistently higher in EPSPsucc than in EPSPfail.
source: The maximum falling slope was consistently higher in EPSPsucc than in EPSPfail (EPSPsucc = 21.1 ± 4.9 vs. EPSPfail = 4.4 ± 1.2 V/s, difference [Δ] = 16.8 ± 4.3 V/s, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 1, Figure 1B left, see also Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: EPSPsucc had higher average EPSP rising slopes than EPSPfail.
source: Still, EPSPsucc had higher average EPSP rising slopes than EPSPfail (EPSPsucc = 9.9 ± 2.2 V/s vs. EPSPfail = 7.5 ± 2.2 V/s, Δ = 2.4 ± 1.5 V/s, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: During spontaneous activity, the failure fraction amounted to 0.28 [0.11, 0.54] with considerable variability between cells.
source: During spontaneous activity, the failure fraction, defined as the proportion of EPSPfail of the ANF input (EPSPsucc + EPSPfail) amounted to 0.28 [0.11, 0.54] with considerable variability between cells (range: 0.01 to 0.91).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data.

claim: Acoustic stimulation at the unit's CF at 50 dB SPL increased the failure fraction to 0.49 [0.41, 0.59].
source: Acoustic stimulation at the unit's CF at 50 dB SPL, i.e. within the excitatory response area, increased the failure fraction to 0.49 [0.41, 0.59] rendering the ANF-SBC synapse less reliable during acoustic stimulation (Δ = 0.18 ± 0.29, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.2, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The ANF-SBC synapse is less reliable during acoustic stimulation than during spontaneous activity.
source: Acoustic stimulation at the unit's CF at 50 dB SPL, i.e. within the excitatory response area, increased the failure fraction to 0.49 [0.41, 0.59] rendering the ANF-SBC synapse less reliable during acoustic stimulation (Δ = 0.18 ± 0.29, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.2, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The increased incidence of failures during acoustic stimulation has been attributed to the activation of inhibitory inputs.
source: The increased incidence of failures during acoustic stimulation has been attributed to the activation of inhibitory inputs (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Kuenzel et al., 2011, 2015; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro experiments showed strong depression at the ANF-SBC synapse.
source: However, also in vitro experiments need to be considered, which showed strong depression at the ANF-SBC synapse (Wang and Manis, 2008; Yang and Xu-Friedman, 2008, 2009; Wang et al., 2010) affecting SBC responsiveness for up to tens of milliseconds (Yang and Xu-Friedman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: In vivo, the impact of depression was shown to be smaller because ongoing spontaneous activity keeps the synapse in a chronically depressed state.
source: Still, in vivo the impact of depression was shown to be smaller, since ongoing spontaneous activity – completely absent in slice recordings – seems to keep the synapse in a chronically depressed state (Hermann et al., 2007; Lorteije et al., 2009; Yang and Xu-Friedman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The in vivo calcium concentration is lower than in artificial cerebrospinal fluid used in slice studies, resulting in lower vesicle release probabilities and smaller depression.
source: Also, the in vivo calcium concentration was reported to be lower than in the artificial cerebrospinal fluid usually used in slice studies resulting in lower vesicle release probabilities and thus smaller depression (Borst, 2010; Kuenzel et al., 2011; Friauf et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EPSP rising slopes showed strong depression for inter-event intervals < 2 ms resulting in high AP failure rates.
source: EPSP rising slopes showed strong depression for inter-event intervals (IEI) < 2 ms resulting in high AP failure rates.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data.

claim: For IEIs > 5 ms, the preceding activity had only a minor influence on EPSP rising slopes.
source: But, already for IEIs > 5 ms, the preceding activity had only a minor influence on EPSP rising slopes (Figure 2A, middle).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with reference to a figure.

claim: Averaging the normalized EPSP slopes across cells showed a facilitating effect for IEI between 2 ms and 20 ms.
source: Averaging the normalized EPSP slopes across cells showed a facilitating effect for IEI between 2 ms and 20 ms (green markers, Figure 2A right).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with reference to a figure.

claim: The threshold EPSP was increased for IEIs < 2 ms, but not for longer IEIs.
source: The threshold EPSP was increased for IEIs < 2 ms, but not for longer IEIs (black line) and the increase in threshold EPSP resulted in an increased failure fraction for IEIs < 2 ms (orange histogram).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data.

claim: The analysis yielded only minor influences of preceding activity on EPSP rising slopes on both EPSPfail and EPSPsucc.
source: The analysis yielded only minor influences of preceding activity on EPSP rising slopes on both EPSPfail (gray) and EPSPsucc (blue) as shown in a representative cell in Figure 2C (left and middle) and also evidenced for the population of recorded units (Spearman's rho EPSPfail = 0.22 ± 0.16 vs. EPSPsucc = 0.24 ± 0.11, Δ = 0.02 ± 0.12, p=0.27, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.09, Figure 2D, see also Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: A small but consistent effect was a positive correlation between preceding ANF activity and EPSP rising slopes indicating a facilitating rather than a depressive influence of higher activity levels in vivo.
source: A small but consistent effect, seen in 61/62 recorded units (98%), was a positive correlation (p<0.001) between preceding ANF activity and EPSP rising slopes indicating a facilitating rather than a depressive influence of higher activity levels in vivo.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: A significant negative correlation was observed between AP amplitude and preceding SBC spiking activity in 92% of the cells.
source: When analyzing the dependence of AP amplitude on preceding SBC spiking activity (exemplary unit shown in Figure 2C right) a significant negative correlation was observed in 92% of the cells (57/62) indicating smaller AP amplitudes after periods of higher SBC activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with reference to figures.

claim: The increased failure fraction during acoustic stimulation in vivo is not explainable by endbulb depression evoked by high firing rates.
source: These results suggest that the increased failure fraction during acoustic stimulation in vivo is not explainable by endbulb depression evoked by high firing rates, highlighting the role of acoustically evoked inhibition on the input-output relationship at the ANF-SBC synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Frequency response areas of SBCs show prominent inhibitory sidebands and reduced firing activity in the excitatory field compared to the ANF input.
source: Frequency response areas (FRA) of SBCs show prominent inhibitory sidebands and reduced firing activity in the excitatory field compared to the ANF input (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Kuenzel et al., 2011; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: About half of the SBCs show pronounced non-monotonic rate-level functions pointing to an impact of inhibition.
source: Also, about half of the SBCs show pronounced non-monotonic rate-level functions pointing to an impact of inhibition (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015; Kuenzel et al., 2015) which has been further classified as 'on-CF inhibition' and 'broadband inhibition' (Winter and Palmer, 1990; Caspary et al., 1994; Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro and modeling studies showed that glycinergic inhibition can elevate the threshold EPSP for AP initiation.
source: In vitro and modeling studies showed that glycinergic inhibition can elevate the threshold EPSP for AP initiation (Xie and Manis, 2013; Kuenzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Elevation in threshold EPSP was observed throughout the FRAs accompanied by an increase in failure fraction.
source: In the present loose-patch recordings, elevation in threshold EPSP (Figure 3Aii/iii) was observed throughout the FRAs (Figure 3Ai/iii) accompanied by an increase in failure fraction (Figure 3Bii).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with reference to figures.

claim: The frequency profile of threshold EPSP elevation closely matched the one of increased failure fraction.
source: The frequency profile of threshold EPSP elevation closely matched the one of increased failure fraction (Figure 3Aii/Bii, Spearman correlation rs = 0.7 [0.4, 0.76], p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 62, U1 = 0.98, population data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory FRAs had similar CFs.
source: Both FRAs had similar CFs, defined as the stimulus frequency at which the lowest sound intensity resulted in a significant increase in ANF firing rate (excitatory) or threshold EPSP (inhibitory) (2.2 ± 0.6 kHz vs. 2.2 ± 0.9 kHz, respectively, Δ = 0.03 ± 0.83 kHz, p=0.77, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.05, Figure 3Ci), but inhibitory FRAs exhibited higher thresholds (excitatory = 4.8 ± 6.1 dB SPL vs. inhibitory = 19.8 ± 16.6 dB SPL, Δ = 15 ± 15.5 dB SPL, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.2, Figure 3Cii, see also Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: Inhibitory FRAs exhibited higher thresholds than excitatory FRAs.
source: Both FRAs had similar CFs, defined as the stimulus frequency at which the lowest sound intensity resulted in a significant increase in ANF firing rate (excitatory) or threshold EPSP (inhibitory) (2.2 ± 0.6 kHz vs. 2.2 ± 0.9 kHz, respectively, Δ = 0.03 ± 0.83 kHz, p=0.77, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.05, Figure 3Ci), but inhibitory FRAs exhibited higher thresholds (excitatory = 4.8 ± 6.1 dB SPL vs. inhibitory = 19.8 ± 16.6 dB SPL, Δ = 15 ± 15.5 dB SPL, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.2, Figure 3Cii, see also Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: Q10 and Q40 values were smaller for the inhibitory FRA compared to the excitatory FRA, indicating reduced frequency selectivity of inhibition.
source: The width of inhibitory and excitatory FRA was determined by calculating Q10 and Q40 values. Both measures were smaller for the inhibitory FRA compared to the excitatory FRA, i.e. inhibition showed reduced frequency selectivity compared to excitation (Q10: excitatory = 2.5 ± 0.6 vs. inhibitory = 1.9 ± 1.1, Δ = 0.5 ± 1.2, p<0.01; Q40: excitatory = 0.96 ± 0.1 vs. inhibitory = 0.6 ± 0.3, Δ = 0.4 ± 0.3, p<0.001, two-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, n = 62, η2 = 0.06, Figure 3Ciii).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: Excitatory FRAs showed distinct low-frequency tails, while inhibitory FRAs were mostly symmetrically arranged around CF.
source: While excitatory FRAs showed distinct low-frequency tails, typical for ANF, inhibitory FRAs were mostly symmetrically arranged around CF, partly covering high-frequency ranges above the excitatory response area (AI excitation = –0.96 ± 0.42 vs AI inhibition = –0.26 ± 0.88, Δ = 0.7 ± 0.97, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.21, Figure 3Civ).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: The rate-level function of the SBC output was markedly flatter and thus less variable with respect to level than the rate-level function of the excitatory ANF input.
source: The rate-level function (RLF) of the SBC output was markedly flatter and thus less variable with respect to level than the rate-level function of the excitatory ANF input.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data.

claim: The output's rate level function had a gain of 1 ± 0.4 which was significantly less than the input's gain of 1.4 ± 0.4.
source: The output's rate level function had a gain of 1 ± 0.4 which was significantly less than the input's (1.4 ± 0.4, Δ = 0.35 ± 0.3, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 62, U1 = 0.1, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Inhibition in SBC is co-tuned with excitation and shows a broader and more symmetric frequency profile.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that inhibition in SBC is co-tuned with excitation and shows a broader and more symmetric frequency profile, which results in flatter rate-level functions and high-frequency inhibitory sidebands at the fringes of the tuning curve (frequently observed in SBC output activity).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Glycine application caused an increase in the number of EPSPs that failed to trigger APs.
source: Glycine was applied iontophoretically, mimicking the putative role of glycinergic inhibition, while monitoring the SBC's spontaneous activity. Indeed, glycine caused an increase in the number of EPSPs that failed to trigger APs, and this specific effect could be blocked by simultaneous application of the glycine receptor antagonist strychnine (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with reference to a figure.

claim: The increase in failure fraction caused by glycine application was accompanied by an elevation in threshold EPSP.
source: This increase in failure fraction was accompanied by an elevation in threshold EPSP (threshold EPSP spont = 6.1 ± 2.2 V/s vs threshold EPSP glycine = 8.4 ± 1.8 V/s, Δ = 2.3 ± 0.9 V/s, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 11, U1 = 0.32, Figure 4B, see also Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The application of the carrier alone had no effect on threshold EPSPs or failure fraction.
source: The application of the carrier alone had neither an effect on threshold EPSPs (threshold EPSP spont = 6.8±1.6 V/s vs. threshold EPSP carrier = 6.8 ± 1.7, Δ = 0 ± 0.3, p=0.89, paired t-test, n = 9, U1 = 0.1, data not shown) nor on failure fraction (failure fraction spont = 0.29 ± 0.17 vs. failure fraction carrier = 0.27 ± 0.16, Δ = 0.03 ± 0.06, p=0.79, paired t-test, n = 9, U1 = 0.11, data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The ANF input firing rates were not influenced by the block of inhibition.
source: The ANF input firing rates were not influenced by the block of inhibition (control = 282 ± 48 Hz vs. strychnine = 283 ± 50 Hz, Δ = 1.2 ± 26.7 Hz, p=0.88, paired t-test, n = 11, U1 = 0.18, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The SBC output rates in the excitatory field were substantially increased under glycine block.
source: The SBC output rates in the excitatory field, however, were substantially increased under glycine block (control = 122 ± 49 Hz vs. strychnine = 192 ± 39 Hz, Δ = 70 ± 47.9 Hz, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 11, U1 = 0.5, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: When glycinergic inhibition was blocked, the threshold EPSP was only affected during acoustic stimulation, but not during spontaneous activity.
source: We next tested if the block of glycinergic inhibition differentially affects the threshold EPSP during spontaneous activity and during acoustic stimulation. When glycinergic inhibition was blocked, the threshold EPSP was only affected during acoustic stimulation, but not during spontaneous activity (interaction drug × stimulus condition, p<0.01, η² = 0.13, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 11, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Acoustic stimulation at CF under control condition resulted in a significant threshold EPSP elevation.
source: Acoustic stimulation at CF under control condition resulted in a significant threshold EPSP elevation (threshold EPSP spont = 5.4 ± 1.6 V/s vs. stim = 8.8 ± 3.1 V/s, Δ = 3.5 ± 2.9 V/s, p<0.01, two-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, n = 11, U1 = 0.41) and this shift was absent when the inhibition was blocked (threshold EPSP spont = 5.9 ± 2 V/s vs. stim = 5.8 ± 1.8 V/s, Δ = 0.1 ± 1.3 V/s, p=0.82, two-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, n = 11, U1 = 0.09, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The threshold EPSP elevation during acoustic stimulation was absent when inhibition was blocked.
source: Acoustic stimulation at CF under control condition resulted in a significant threshold EPSP elevation (threshold EPSP spont = 5.4 ± 1.6 V/s vs. stim = 8.8 ± 3.1 V/s, Δ = 3.5 ± 2.9 V/s, p<0.01, two-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, n = 11, U1 = 0.41) and this shift was absent when the inhibition was blocked (threshold EPSP spont = 5.9 ± 2 V/s vs. stim = 5.8 ± 1.8 V/s, Δ = 0.1 ± 1.3 V/s, p=0.82, two-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, n = 11, U1 = 0.09, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: In the absence of acoustic stimulation, the block of glycinergic inhibition had no effect on output rates or threshold EPSP.
source: In the absence of acoustic stimulation, the block of glycinergic inhibition had no effect on output rates (control = 51 ± 26 Hz vs. strychnine = 49 ± 20 Hz, Δ = 1.6 ± 18.5 Hz, p=0.79, two-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, n = 11, U1 = 0.14, data not shown), and threshold EPSP (control = 5.5 ± 2.5 V/s vs strychnine = 5.6 ± 2.6 V/s, Δ = 0.03 ± 0.16 V/s, p=0.53, two-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, n = 11, U1 = 0.09, Figure 4Eii).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Glycinergic inhibition has a major role in acoustically evoked signal processing, but a negligible impact during spontaneous activity.
source: These data suggest a major role of glycinergic inhibition in acoustically evoked signal processing, but a negligible impact during spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Previous studies directly comparing the ANF input and SBC output showed an increase in temporal precision attributed to inhibition.
source: Previous studies directly comparing the ANF input and SBC output showed an increase in temporal precision which has been attributed to the impact of inhibition (Dehmel et al., 2010; Kuenzel et al., 2011; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The AP failure fraction increased from 0.27 ± 0.22 in the absence of acoustic stimulation to 0.43 ± 0.18 during SAM stimulation.
source: The AP failure fraction increased from 0.27 ± 0.22 in the absence of acoustic stimulation to 0.43 ± 0.18 during SAM stimulation (Δ = 0.16 ± 0.18, p<0.01, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 14, η² = 0.11, data not shown) and was independent of modulation frequency (factor frequency: p=0.19, η² < 0.01; interaction stimulus type × frequency: p=0.27, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, η² < 0.01, n = 14).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The SBC output exhibited consistently higher vector strength compared to its ANF input during SAM stimulation.
source: The SBC output exhibited consistently higher VS compared to its ANF input (Δ = 0.06 ± 0.04, p<0.001, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 14, η² = 0.09, Figure 5D, see also Figure 5—source data 1), and decreased for modulation frequencies above 200 Hz (factor frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.09; interaction signal type × frequency: p<0.05, η² < 0.01, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 14).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Modulation depth was considerably higher at the SBC output during SAM stimulation.
source: Modulation depth was considerably higher at the SBC output (Δ = 0.04 ± 0.04, p<0.001, η² = 0.09) and decreased with modulation frequency (factor frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.08; interaction signal type × frequency: p=0.12, η² < 0.01, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 14).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In 97% of all recorded cells, the SBC output exhibited a higher level of reproducibility during SAM stimulation.
source: In 97% (33/34) of all recorded cells, the SBC output exhibited a higher level of reproducibility (units above line of equality, Figure 8Bii). Also, the population analysis yielded a significantly higher reproducibility of the SBC output than the ANF input (ANF = 0.46 [0.37, 0.65] vs. SBC = 0.83 [0.48, 1.3], Δ = 0.35 [0.12, 0.73], p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 34, U1 = 0.18, Figure 8Biii).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: For SFM stimulation, the SBC output showed higher vector strength compared to their ANF input.
source: For SFM stimulation – same as for SAM - the SBC output showed higher VS compared to their ANF input (Δ = 0.14 ± 0.09, p<0.001, η² = 0.21, see also Figure 6—source data 1) (Figure 6D left) (factor frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.48; interaction signal type × frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.03, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 19).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The modulation depth was considerably higher for the SBC output than the ANF input during SFM stimulation.
source: The modulation depth was considerably higher for the SBC output than the ANF input (Figure 6D midleft; Δ = 0.24 ± 0.16, p<0.001, η² = 0.28) and strongly depended on the modulation frequency (factor frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.37; interaction signal type × frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.03, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 19).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Signal reproducibility was higher for the SBC output than the ANF input during SFM stimulation.
source: The same holds for signal reproducibility (Figure 6D midright; Δ = 1.9 ± 1.2, p<0.001, η² = 0.38) which also showed prominent frequency dependency (factor frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.26; interaction signal type × frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.02, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 19).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The normalized correlation between SFM stimulus envelope and neural response revealed a lower reproducibility for the SBC output compared to the ANF input.
source: Unlike the previous measures, the normalized correlation between SFM stimulus envelope and neural response revealed a lower reproducibility for the SBC output compared to the ANF input (Figure 6D right; Δ = 0.02 ± 0.03, p<0.001, η² = 0.06), and the difference also holds with respect to the effect of modulation frequency (factor frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.43; interaction signal type × frequency: p<0.001, η² = 0.03, two-way RM ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, n = 19).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The SBC output shows temporally increased precision and higher response reproducibility during SFM stimulation.
source: Overall, these data suggest that – same as for the SAM stimuli – the SBC output shows temporally increased precision and higher response reproducibility during SFM stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Summing all the positive regions in the STRF revealed a significant reduction from ANFs to SBCs.
source: Summing all the positive regions revealed a significant reduction from ANFs to SBCs (ANF = 0.38 [0.37, 0.41] vs. SBC = 0.33 [0.31, 0.36], Δ = 0.05 [0.03, 0.07], p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 34, U1 = 0.16, Figure 7C, see also Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The summed negative region in the SBC output was significantly larger in magnitude than the ANF input.
source: Similarly, the summed negative region in the SBC output was significantly larger in magnitude than the ANF input (ANF = 0.18 [0.15, 0.23] vs. SBC = 0.25 [0.18, 0.29], Δ = 0.04 [0.02, 0.07], p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 34, U1 = 0.1, Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The spectral tuning, measured as half-width of the excitatory region, was reduced at the SBC output compared to ANF input.
source: The spectral tuning, measured as half-width of the excitatory region, was reduced at the SBC output compared to ANF input, suggesting a spectrally sharper tuning at the SBC output (ANF = 1.2 [0.9, 1.4] octaves vs. SBC = 1 [0.8, 1.2] octaves, Δ = 0.1 [0, 0.2], p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 34, U1 = 0.01, Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Temporal precision, measured as the half-width of the excitatory region, was somewhat higher for the SBC output, but did not reach statistical significance.
source: Temporal precision, measured correspondingly as the half-width of the excitatory region, was somewhat higher for the SBC output, but did not reach statistical significance (ANF = 2.2 [1.8, 3.4] ms vs. SBC = 2.0 [1.8, 3.1] ms, Δ = 0.08 [-0.1, 0.18], p=0.16, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 34, U1 = 0.03, Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: The reduction in the STRF outlasted the excitatory region for up to ~10 ms relative to the onset of the excitatory signal component.
source: As mentioned above, the reduction in the STRF outlasted the excitatory region for up to ~10 ms relative to the onset of the excitatory signal component.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data.

claim: The STRF analysis confirmed the presence of inhibition co-tuned with excitation, exhibiting a longer-lasting time-course of about 10 ms.
source: Overall, the STRF analysis confirmed the presence of inhibition co-tuned with excitation, exhibiting a longer-lasting time-course of about 10 ms with respect to the onset of the excitatory signal component.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Inhibition acts only marginally above or below the neuron's excitatory receptive field and results in only a slight spectral sharpening of the SBC output.
source: Consequently, also under dynamic broadband stimulation, inhibition is confirmed to only marginally act above or below the neuron's excitatory receptive field and results in only a slight spectral sharpening of the SBC output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The population analysis revealed significantly larger temporal sparsity in the SBC output than in its ANF input.
source: The population analysis revealed significantly larger temporal sparsity in the SBC output than in its ANF input (ANF = 0.22 ± 0.08 vs. SBC = 0.31 ± 0.13, Δ = 0.09 ± 0.08, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 34, U1 = 0.15, Figure 8Aiii, see also Figure 8–source data).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Blocking glycinergic inhibition in vivo by strychnine deteriorated the improved sparsity of the SBC output and rendered it similar to the ANF input.
source: Blocking glycinergic inhibition in vivo by strychnine (n = 12) deteriorated the improved sparsity of the SBC output and rendered it similar to the ANF input (p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed rank test), while the ANF input remained unchanged.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Application of strychnine impoverished reproducibility in the SBC output significantly compared to the control condition.
source: Application of strychnine impoverished reproducibility in the SBC output (light blue) significantly compared to the control condition (dark blue; p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed rank test). The reproducibility of the ANF input (orange) was not influenced by blocking the inhibition (light orange).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Blocking inhibition increases temporal dispersion of the SBC output to the level of the ANF input.
source: As above, blocking inhibition increases temporal dispersion of the SBC output to the level of the ANF input (iv, p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Purely divisive inhibition does not improve sparsity, reproducibility or temporal precision.
source: Purely divisive inhibition, corresponding to a scaling of the PSTH, does not improve sparsity, reproducibility or temporal precision (Figure 9, purple, Δsparsity = 0 ± 0, p=0.99, Δreproducibility = 0.01 ± 0.02, p=0.25, Δtemporal dispersion = 0.05 ± 0.41, p=0.89, n = 34, one-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted, see also Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of simulation results with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: A purely subtractive inhibition matches the qualitative effects in the data well, improving all three properties (sparsity, reproducibility, temporal precision).
source: On the other hand, a purely subtractive inhibition matches the qualitative effects in the data well, i.e. improves all three properties (Figure 9, green, Δsparsity = 0.24 ± 0.08, p<0.001, Δreproducibility = 1.06 ± 0.73, p<0.001, Δtemporal dispersion = 1.8 ± 1.3 ms, p<0.001, n = 34, one-way RM ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted).
evidence: This is a direct statement of simulation results with statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: A temporally unspecific, subtractive effect of inhibition might be sufficient to explain the improvement in sparsity, reproducibility, and temporal precision.
source: A temporally unspecific, subtractive effect of inhibition might, therefore, be sufficient to explain the improvement in sparsity, reproducibility, and temporal precision.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Glycinergic inhibition shapes SBC responses to become sparser and more reproducible for a broad range of stimulation conditions.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that glycinergic inhibition shapes SBC responses to become sparser and more reproducible for a broad range of stimulation conditions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's results.

claim: Inhibition acts largely co-tuned with excitation, although its latency and duration exceed the excitatory input.
source: We find inhibition to act largely co-tuned with excitation, although its latency and duration exceed the excitatory input, similar to the respective relationship found in the cortex.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's results.

claim: Glycinergic inhibition takes a functional role as a gain control and a signal quality enhancer.
source: Therefore, we propose glycinergic inhibition to take a functional role as a gain control and a signal quality enhancer, which optimizes the SBC output for the subsequent high-fidelity integration for sound localization in the MSO and LSO (see below).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's results.

claim: The endbulb of Held–SBC synapse operates close to AP threshold and shows variable reliability which is strongly influenced by acoustically evoked inhibition.
source: In summary, the endbulb of Held–SBC synapse seems to operate close to AP threshold and shows variable reliability which is strongly influenced by acoustically evoked inhibition (see also Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Kuenzel et al., 2011; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The present data suggest that inhibition at SBCs is broadband and on-CF.
source: While the observed frequency response areas are consistent with previous reports, we did not observe two distinct types of inhibition as reported earlier, i.e. broadband vs. on-CF inhibition (Caspary et al., 1994; Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002). Instead, the present data suggest that inhibition at SBCs is broadband and on-CF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: SBCs receive inhibitory inputs both on their somata and dendrites.
source: SBCs receive inhibitory inputs both on their somata and dendrites (Gómez-Nieto and Rubio, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both glycine and GABA receptors are present on SBCs, with GABA playing a secondary role.
source: Both glycine and GABA receptors were shown to be present, with the latter playing a secondary role as demonstrated in slice experiments (Nerlich et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lack of threshold EPSP elevation during the block of glycinergic inhibition suggests only a minor influence of the GABAergic component during tone burst stimulation.
source: Consistent with the slice data, the lack of threshold EPSP elevation during the block of glycinergic inhibition suggests only a minor influence of the GABAergic component during tone burst stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Glycine has a substantial influence in shaping transmission at the SBC junction.
source: Overall, we find glycine to have a substantial influence in shaping transmission at the SBC junction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Glycinergic inhibition is neither purely subtractive nor purely divisive.
source: Glycinergic inhibition has previously been demonstrated to be neither purely subtractive nor purely divisive (Kuenzel et al., 2011; 2015; Nerlich et al., 2014b) and act with a short delay of ~3 ms on time scales of ~10–15 ms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An increase in temporal sparsity can be advantageous because the information per spike is increased.
source: Generally, if the information in the response is largely maintained, an increase in temporal sparsity can be advantageous for mainly three reasons. First, the information per spike is increased (Barlow, 1972, 2012; Olshausen and Field, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A reduction in the number of spikes reduces the energetic load on the system.
source: Third, a reduction in the number of spikes reduces the energetic load on the system (Levy and Baxter, 1996; Baddeley et al., 1997; Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Graham and Field, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SBCs provide the indispensable temporally precise excitatory inputs to the interaural time difference based sound localization in the MSO.
source: SBCs provide the indispensable temporally precise excitatory inputs to the interaural time difference based sound localization in the MSO.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the auditory system.

claim: Physiological and modeling studies suggest the neurons in the MSO act as coincidence detectors by primarily relying on the precise spike timing of binaural inputs.
source: Both, physiological and modeling studies suggest the neurons in the MSO act as coincidence detectors by primarily relying on the precise spike timing of binaural inputs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969; Yin and Chan, 1990; Franken et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: With the MSO neurons acting as coincidence detectors, sparse excitatory inputs would lead to an improved signal-to-noise ratio of the correlation.
source: With the MSO neurons acting as coincidence detectors (Couchman et al., 2010; Plauška et al., 2016), sparse excitatory inputs would lead to an improved signal-to-noise ratio of the correlation, i.e. of its peak in relation to the common floor of correlation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: The effective gain control achieved through acoustically evoked inhibition will allow the MSO to retain a similar level of binaural sensitivity across a wide range of sound levels and stimuli.
source: Equally important, the effective gain control achieved through the acoustically evoked inhibition will allow the MSO to retain a similar level of binaural sensitivity across a wide range of sound levels and stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Studies comparing ANF and AVCN neurons in the cat reported increased reproducibility in neurons of the AVCN.
source: The observed increase in reproducibility in SBC output compared to the ANF input is consistent with previously reported population data. Studies comparing ANF and AVCN neurons (most likely spherical or globular bushy cells) in the cat reported increased reproducibility in neurons of the AVCN (Louage et al., 2005; van der Heijden et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most models of pitch perception are based on or related to an autocorrelation of neuronal activity and rely on temporal precision and reproducibility.
source: Most models of pitch perception are based on or related to an autocorrelation of neuronal activity and rely on temporal precision and reproducibility (Licklider, 1951; Meddis and Hewitt, 1991; Cariani and Delgutte, 1996; Yost, 1996; de Cheveigné, 1998; Denham, 2005; Joris, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The improvement of temporal precision and reproducibility at the ANF-SBC synapse might support the neuronal processing of pitch.
source: The improvement of both characteristics at the ANF-SBC synapse might support the neuronal processing of pitch, but experimental evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Other transmitters such as acetylcholine or norepinephrine have modulatory effects on the SBC activity.
source: Other transmitters such as acetylcholine (Fujino and Oertel, 2001; Goyer et al., 2016) or norepinephrine (Kössl and Vater, 1989; Rothman and Manis, 2003) have modulatory effects on the SBC activity, but their effect on precisely-timed signal processing is not yet fully understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several nuclei have been suggested to provide the inhibitory inputs to SBCs.
source: Several nuclei have been suggested to provide the inhibitory inputs to SBCs.
evidence: This is a statement of existing knowledge in the field.

claim: The present data suggest the inhibitory source to feature a broad, symmetrically shaped tuning.
source: The present data suggest the inhibitory source to feature a broad, symmetrically shaped tuning, consistent with an integration over a wide set of primary tuned inhibitory cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Campagnola and Manis (2014) showed directly that bushy cells receive symmetric inhibition from within the CN.
source: In a recent study, Campagnola and Manis (2014) showed directly that bushy cells receive symmetric inhibition from within the CN.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ~1 ms delay of the onset of acoustically evoked inhibition compared to the onset of excitation suggests a single additional synaptic relay.
source: Further, the ~1 ms delay of the onset of acoustically evoked inhibition compared to the onset of excitation (Kuenzel et al., 2011; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015) suggests a single additional synaptic relay.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Both the broadly tuned D-stellate cells in the AVCN and the tuberculoventral cells in the DCN are candidate sources of inhibition to SBCs.
source: Together, both the broadly tuned D-stellate cells in the AVCN and the tuberculoventral cells in the DCN are candidate sources (Wickesberg and Oertel, 1990; Saint Marie et al., 1991; Campagnola and Manis, 2014), as well as cells in the lateral nucleus of the trapezoid body (Smith et al., 1991; Schofield and Cant, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acoustically evoked inhibition on SBC renders the ANF-SBC junction less reliable with respect to signal transmission.
source: In summary, while acoustically evoked inhibition on SBC renders the ANF-SBC junction less reliable with respect to signal transmission, it enables sparser and more reproducible SBC sound encoding, which might be of relevance for subsequent localization of sound sources.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's results.

claim: Acoustically evoked inhibition enables sparser and more reproducible SBC sound encoding.
source: In summary, while acoustically evoked inhibition on SBC renders the ANF-SBC junction less reliable with respect to signal transmission, it enables sparser and more reproducible SBC sound encoding, which might be of relevance for subsequent localization of sound sources.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's results.

claim: All experiments were performed at the Neurobiology Laboratories of the Faculty of Bioscience, Pharmacy and Psychology of the University of Leipzig.
source: All experiments were performed at the Neurobiology Laboratories of the Faculty of Bioscience, Pharmacy and Psychology of the University of Leipzig (Germany), approved by the Saxonian District Government, Leipzig (TVV 06/09), and conducted according to the European Communities Council Directive (86/609/EEC).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedures.

claim: Data were collected from 42 Mongolian gerbils of either sex aged 4 to 12 weeks.
source: Data were collected from 42 Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) of either sex aged 4 to 12 weeks (P43 ± 13).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.
